newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Weather fears prey on world grain markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Weather fears prey on world grain markets.

text.p: Chicago benchmark wheat futures jumped back above the psychological threshold of $4 per bushel on Friday on fears of crop damage from a late snap of winter cold in the United States.

In Europe, although alarm bells weren't jangling yet, concern in the wheat trade also mounted because of the weather -- in that case over a drought -- further underlining the present risk of climatic hazard to the world's food supply.
Bumper 1996 harvests barely lifted global grain stocks from 20-year lows blamed on previous drought in Russia, Australia and North Africa.
Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures opened sharply higher, boosted by a US Department of Agriculture cut in stock forecasts as well as the risk of cold weather.

Forecasts called for temperatures to fall below freezing as far south as Texas, putting developing crops in Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas at risk, meteorologists said. Sustained cold temperatures can cause winterkill in wheat.
USDA on Friday cut wheat year-ending stocks to 460 million bushels and raised US exports by 35 million bushels to 985 million due to stronger-than-expected late season sales.
Nearby May CBOT wheat futures rose more than 12-1/2 cents to top $4.05 per bushel. Prices had last sunk below $4 at the start of April.
USDA also cut soybean stock forecasts but soybean product prices soon shed early gains on traders' views that demand was also easing.
Drought, however, cut forecasts for the important Brazil soybean crop just as dry weather also became an obsession among Europe's grain traders over the past week with no significant rain forecast.

Fears for the developing new crop, hit by drought in some of the most important growing areas, have driven prices higher. Dealers in Spain said the drought played havoc with prices. British wheat futures have risen, led by the new crop.
French traders' fears for the new crop were made worse by a forecast Thursday showing no rain for at least the next week and imposition of some controls on water use in irrigation.
But Germany is unscathed. It is dry, but the grains market is not getting over-concerned, one explained. Prices in northern Germany are steady.
Elsewhere in world commodity markets, crude oil prices steadied on concerns that tensions between the West and Iran might at some point affect supply.
Base metals eased on chart-based selling in thin volume. Gold eased on speculative selling and US data suggesting stronger-than-expected inflation.
